name: BigQuery
description: Protects the `bq` CLI and GoogleSQL against dataset drops, table \ overwrites, unfiltered DML, and settings that shorten the time-travel \ recovery window

destructive_patterns.name: bq-rm-recursive
destructive_patterns.description: bq rm -r deletes a dataset and every table, view, and routine inside it.
destructive_patterns.explanation:
Recursive removal deletes the dataset together with all of its contents in one \ call. Individual tables can sometimes be recovered from time travel within \ 2-7 days, but the dataset itself cannot be restored once dropped.

\ Inspect the contents first: \ bq ls <project>:<dataset>

destructive_patterns.name: bq-rm-transfer-config
destructive_patterns.description: bq rm --transfer_config deletes a scheduled query or data transfer.
destructive_patterns.explanation:
Removing a transfer config stops the scheduled load or query silently — the \ next run simply never happens, and the schedule, destination, and parameters \ are gone with it.

\ Record the config before removing it: \ bq show --transfer_config <resource-name>

destructive_patterns.name: bq-rm-reservation
destructive_patterns.description: bq rm --reservation removes purchased capacity and can change query cost and performance.
destructive_patterns.explanation:
Reservations and capacity commitments are billing objects. Removing one moves \ the affected workloads onto on-demand pricing, which changes both cost and \ concurrency behaviour immediately.

\ Inspect the reservation first: \ bq show --reservation --location=<location> <name>

destructive_patterns.name: bq-rm
destructive_patterns.description: bq rm deletes a table, view, model, or dataset.
destructive_patterns.explanation:
Deletion is immediate. A table may be recoverable from time travel within the \ dataset's window (2-7 days) using the `@<epoch_ms>` decorator, but only if \ nothing recreates the name in the meantime; datasets and models have no such \ recovery.

\ Confirm the target first: \ bq show <project>:<dataset>.<table>

destructive_patterns.name: bq-load-replace
destructive_patterns.description: bq load --replace overwrites all existing data in the destination table.
destructive_patterns.explanation:
`--replace` truncates the destination table before loading. If the source file \ is wrong, short, or malformed, the previous contents are already gone and only \ time travel can recover them.

\ Safer alternative: \ - bq load --noreplace: append instead of overwriting \ - load into a staging table first, then swap

destructive_patterns.name: bq-query-replace
destructive_patterns.description: bq query --replace overwrites the destination table with the query result.
destructive_patterns.explanation:
`--replace` discards the destination table's current contents before writing \ the result. A query that returns fewer rows than expected silently destroys \ the difference.

\ Safer alternative: \ - bq query --append_table: add rows instead of replacing them \ - bq query --dry_run: check what the query would process first

destructive_patterns.name: bq-cp-force
destructive_patterns.description: bq cp -f overwrites the destination table without prompting.
destructive_patterns.explanation:
`-f` suppresses the overwrite confirmation, so an existing destination table is \ replaced silently. Copying onto the wrong destination is not detectable after \ the fact except through time travel.

\ Check whether the destination already exists: \ bq show <project>:<dataset>.<table>

destructive_patterns.name: bq-mk-force
destructive_patterns.description: bq mk -f overwrites an existing table definition.
destructive_patterns.explanation:
`bq mk -f` succeeds when the object already exists, replacing its definition \ rather than failing. Recreating a table this way drops the existing rows.

\ Check first: \ bq show <project>:<dataset>.<table>

destructive_patterns.name: bq-update-time-travel
destructive_patterns.description: bq update --max_time_travel_hours shortens the only window in which deleted BigQuery data can be recovered.
destructive_patterns.explanation:
Time travel (48-168 hours) is BigQuery's only undo. Lowering it discards \ history immediately and irreversibly: data older than the new window cannot be \ recovered afterwards, including data you have not yet noticed is missing. This \ destroys the recovery path itself rather than any single table.

\ Take a snapshot before shortening the window: \ bq cp <dataset>.<table>@<epoch_ms> <dataset>.<table>_backup

destructive_patterns.name: bq-update-expiration
destructive_patterns.description: bq update --expiration schedules automatic deletion of tables or partitions.
destructive_patterns.explanation:
An expiration is a deferred delete. Setting one on a dataset applies to tables \ created afterwards; setting one on a table schedules that table's removal. The \ deletion happens later, without a prompt, and is easy to forget was configured.

\ Inspect the current setting: \ bq show --format=prettyjson <project>:<dataset>

destructive_patterns.name: bq-cancel
destructive_patterns.description: bq cancel stops a running job, which may leave a partial load or export.
destructive_patterns.explanation:
Cancelling a load or export mid-flight can leave the destination in a partial \ state: some files written, some rows loaded. Check what the job is doing before \ stopping it.

\ Inspect the job first: \ bq show --job=true <job-id>

destructive_patterns.name: drop-schema
destructive_patterns.description: DROP SCHEMA removes a BigQuery dataset and everything inside it.
destructive_patterns.explanation:
In GoogleSQL a *dataset* is a SCHEMA, so this is the dataset-level catastrophe \ rather than a namespace tidy-up. With CASCADE it removes every table, view, and \ routine in the dataset. Individual tables may be recoverable from time travel \ for 2-7 days; the dataset is not.

\ List the contents first: \ bq ls <project>:<dataset>

destructive_patterns.name: drop-snapshot-table
destructive_patterns.description: DROP SNAPSHOT TABLE destroys a point-in-time backup.
destructive_patterns.explanation: A table snapshot is often the backup taken precisely because time travel is too \ short. Dropping it removes the recovery point itself, and unlike the source \ table it has no time-travel window of its own.

destructive_patterns.name: drop-materialized-view-or-external-table
destructive_patterns.description: DROP MATERIALIZED VIEW / EXTERNAL TABLE removes a derived or federated object.
destructive_patterns.explanation: A materialized view holds precomputed data that must be rebuilt, which costs a \ full refresh; an external table definition carries the schema and source URIs \ needed to read the underlying files. Neither the data nor the definition is \ recoverable from time travel.

destructive_patterns.name: drop-routine
destructive_patterns.description: DROP FUNCTION/PROCEDURE/TABLE FUNCTION removes a routine other queries may depend on.
destructive_patterns.explanation:
Routine definitions are not covered by time travel. Anything calling the routine \ — scheduled queries, views, downstream jobs — starts failing at its next run.

\ Capture the definition first: \ SELECT ddl FROM `<project>.<dataset>.INFORMATION_SCHEMA.ROUTINES`

destructive_patterns.name: drop-model
destructive_patterns.description: DROP MODEL deletes a trained BigQuery ML model.
destructive_patterns.explanation:
A model is not covered by time travel and cannot be restored — rebuilding it \ means re-running training over the original data, which costs both money and \ hours, and reproduces the result only if that training data still exists in \ the same form.

\ Copy it first: \ bq cp <dataset>.<model> <dataset>.<model>_backup

destructive_patterns.name: drop-all-row-access-policies
destructive_patterns.description: DROP ROW ACCESS POLICY removes row-level security from a table.
destructive_patterns.explanation: This does not delete data — it exposes it. Every row previously filtered by a \ policy becomes visible to anyone with table access, which is a disclosure event \ rather than a data-loss one, and it is silent.

destructive_patterns.name: drop-search-index
destructive_patterns.description: DROP SEARCH INDEX removes an index that must be fully rebuilt.
destructive_patterns.explanation: Rebuilding a search or vector index over a large table is expensive and not \ instantaneous; queries relying on it degrade to full scans in the meantime.

destructive_patterns.name: drop-capacity-or-reservation
destructive_patterns.description: DROP CAPACITY/RESERVATION/ASSIGNMENT changes billing and query capacity.
destructive_patterns.explanation: These are billing objects. Dropping one moves affected workloads to on-demand \ pricing immediately, changing both cost and concurrency.

destructive_patterns.name: drop-view
destructive_patterns.description: DROP VIEW removes a view definition.
destructive_patterns.explanation:
View definitions are not covered by time travel. Downstream queries and \ dashboards referencing the view break at their next run.

\ Capture the definition first: \ SELECT view_definition FROM `<project>.<dataset>.INFORMATION_SCHEMA.VIEWS`

destructive_patterns.name: drop-table
destructive_patterns.description: DROP TABLE removes a table and its data.
destructive_patterns.explanation:
The table may be recoverable from time travel within the dataset's window \ (2-7 days) via `<table>@<epoch_ms>`, but only if nothing recreates the name in \ the meantime — recreating it starts a fresh history and forecloses recovery.

\ Snapshot before dropping: \ bq cp <dataset>.<table>@<epoch_ms> <dataset>.<table>_backup

destructive_patterns.name: alter-table-drop-column
destructive_patterns.description: ALTER TABLE DROP COLUMN removes a column and its data.
destructive_patterns.explanation: Dropping a column deletes its values. Time travel recovers the whole table to a \ prior point rather than restoring one column, so recovery means reconstructing \ the table.

destructive_patterns.name: alter-set-expiration
destructive_patterns.description: SET OPTIONS(expiration_timestamp) schedules automatic deletion.
destructive_patterns.explanation: An expiration timestamp is a deferred delete: the object disappears at that time \ with no further prompt. Setting it in the past deletes immediately.

destructive_patterns.name: alter-table-rename
destructive_patterns.description: ALTER TABLE RENAME TO breaks every reference to the old table name.
destructive_patterns.explanation: Renaming is not itself data loss, but views, scheduled queries, and downstream \ jobs referencing the old name fail at their next run, and a later `CREATE TABLE` \ reusing the old name makes the break silent.

destructive_patterns.name: create-or-replace-routine
destructive_patterns.description: CREATE OR REPLACE FUNCTION/PROCEDURE overwrites an existing routine definition.
destructive_patterns.explanation: The previous definition is discarded with no version history. If the new body is \ wrong, the old one must be reconstructed from source control or memory.

destructive_patterns.name: create-or-replace-table
destructive_patterns.description: CREATE OR REPLACE TABLE discards the existing table and its data.
destructive_patterns.explanation:
This is a drop and recreate in one statement: the old rows are gone before the \ new ones are written. A query that produces fewer rows than expected destroys \ the difference silently.

\ Safer alternative: \ - CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS: fails instead of overwriting \ - write to a staging table and swap after verifying

destructive_patterns.name: load-data-overwrite
destructive_patterns.description: LOAD DATA OVERWRITE replaces all existing data in the destination table.
destructive_patterns.explanation:
`OVERWRITE` truncates the destination before loading. If the source is wrong or \ short, the previous contents are already gone.

\ Safer alternative: \ - LOAD DATA INTO: append instead of replacing

destructive_patterns.name: export-data-overwrite
destructive_patterns.description: EXPORT DATA with overwrite=true replaces files at the destination URI.
destructive_patterns.explanation: Existing objects under the destination prefix in Cloud Storage are replaced. If \ the bucket is not versioned, the previous export is unrecoverable.

destructive_patterns.name: truncate-table
destructive_patterns.description: TRUNCATE TABLE removes every row in the table.
destructive_patterns.explanation: All rows are deleted while the schema stays in place. Recovery is time travel \ only, within the dataset's 2-7 day window.

destructive_patterns.name: delete-all-rows
destructive_patterns.description: DELETE ... WHERE TRUE removes every row in the table.
destructive_patterns.explanation:
In GoogleSQL a WHERE clause is mandatory on DELETE, so `WHERE TRUE` is the \ idiomatic way to spell "delete everything" — it is a full-table delete, not a \ filtered one. Recovery is time travel only.

\ Check the blast radius first: \ SELECT COUNT(*) FROM `<table>` WHERE <your-predicate>

destructive_patterns.name: update-all-rows
destructive_patterns.description: UPDATE ... WHERE TRUE rewrites every row in the table.
destructive_patterns.explanation:
`WHERE TRUE` is the idiomatic full-table spelling in GoogleSQL, where the WHERE \ clause is mandatory. Every row is rewritten, and the prior values are recoverable \ only through time travel.

\ Check the blast radius first: \ SELECT COUNT(*) FROM `<table>` WHERE <your-predicate>

destructive_patterns.name: merge-delete-not-matched-by-source
destructive_patterns.description: MERGE ... WHEN NOT MATCHED BY SOURCE THEN DELETE removes every target row absent from the source.
destructive_patterns.explanation:
The delete is driven by what the source query returns. If the source is empty, \ filtered, or partially loaded, this deletes most or all of the target table — \ and the statement looks routine in review.

\ Check what the source actually returns first: \ SELECT COUNT(*) FROM (<source-query>)
